questions.prompt: Explain how ww4 decides whether a caller may create an issue in a project: which two role sources are consulted, how they combine, and at which layers the decision is enforced.

keyPoints.text: The organisation role is checked first: ORG_OWNER and ORG_ADMIN pass every project permission whether or not they hold a membership in that project.
Anyone else needs a project membership row; with no project role the check answers false outright.
With a project role, the answer is a lookup in the role's permission list, and the OBSERVER list carries view, comment and filter creation but not issue:create.

Both roles are captured once per request into a ProjectAccessContext (the org role from the session's memberships, the project role from the user's membership row), and createIssue takes that object as given, so its own re-check reads the same snapshot rather than the database.
The route demands issue:create through requireProjectAccess before it even parses the request body.
createIssue asserts the same permission again as its first statement, so a caller that reaches the service without the route still gets refused.
The project-role grants are a constant in code, not data: changing what an OBSERVER may do is a deploy, and no database row can grant issue:create beyond the roles the table lists.

questions.prompt: Walk through what createIssue validates against the project's own configuration before any write, and why those checks cannot live in the request schema.

keyPoints.text: The payload by itself is not enough evidence: validity depends on what this project has defined.
keyPoints.quote: An issue payload alone cannot determine whether a custom field is valid.

keyPoints.text: The zod schema can only shape each custom value as a field id plus an unknown value (at most twenty entries); typing it requires the definitions.
validateCustomFieldValues refuses a field id the project does not define, an empty value for a required field, a value of the wrong primitive type, and a select value outside the configured options.
A second pass over the definitions catches a required field the client omitted entirely, which the per-value loop can never see.
An assignee must be a member of this project, checked with an organisation- and project-scoped member query.
The starting status is not a client field at all; the server takes it from the workflow.
keyPoints.quote: the client does not choose the initial workflow status; project configuration supplies it.

keyPoints.text: Nothing in the database guarantees exactly one initial status: the rule is a superRefine on the project payload, and requireInitialWorkflowStatus takes the first flagged status with .find, so a second flagged status written outside that schema is silently ignored.

questions.prompt: Defend or indict the ordering in ww4's createIssue, where every check finishes before db.$transaction opens: what does that order buy, and what does it leave unproven?

keyPoints.text: A refused request never reaches the transaction, so it allocates no sequence number and writes no partial issue; the transaction only opens after the initial status is resolved.
The runtime test pins that: the permission refusal records no calls at all, and the missing-workflow and no-initial-status refusals record only the setup read.
Inside the transaction sit only writes: sequence, issue row, custom values, the ISSUE_CREATED activity and the automation event, all on the same tx client.

Sequence allocation is MAX(sequenceNumber) + 1 read inside the transaction at the default isolation level (no isolationLevel is set anywhere in src), so two concurrent creates in one project can both read the same maximum.

The loser then hits @@unique([projectId, sequenceNumber]) with Prisma's P2002, and handleRouteError only recognises ZodError and AppError, so the caller gets the generic 500 instead of a retry or a 409.
The repo's own review lists the fixes: a per-project counter row updated with UPDATE ... RETURNING, a retry on P2002, or SERIALIZABLE isolation with retry; none is in the code at this commit.
The assignee's membership is checked before the transaction opens and never re-read on the transaction client, so a member removed in between can still be assigned the new issue.
